title: A predictive science of human–computer interaction

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a transferable scientific account of how people discover, learn, misunderstand, and adapt to computer interfaces. Given an unfamiliar interface, a task, and information about its users and setting, it would produce quantitative predictions about behavior: how long tasks take, which errors occur, how performance changes with practice, and how people respond when the interface changes. The ambition is to predict interaction across interface families without hand-coding a new user strategy for every design.

Such an account would connect perception, action, memory, learning, prior knowledge, and social context while representing differences among users. Computational rationality offers a foundation: it models behavior as adaptation to an environment under limits on cognitive and physical resources. The broader proposed capability would also need to predict how adaptation develops, how experience transfers to unfamiliar interfaces, and when predictions become unreliable. Explicit uncertainty and limits of applicability are proposed requirements for this innovation.

significance.text: If demonstrated, this capability would make interface design substantially more predictive. Designers could evaluate proposed changes before observing users of those designs, including changes that cause people to adopt different strategies. Its direct contribution would be testable predictions of behavior under stated conditions, extending the usefulness of models beyond explaining or fitting previously observed interactions. The 2022 computational-rationality paper provides a technical basis for this possibility through parameterized simulations of responses to hypothetical design interventions.

Conditional downstream possibilities include design tools that identify likely learning difficulties, compare alternative interaction methods, or anticipate errors before deployment. Safer systems and more accessible interfaces could follow if those predictions were implemented and validated in their particular settings. These are potential applications, not demonstrated consequences of the supplied research; reliable behavioral prediction alone would not establish safety, accessibility, or an appropriate design objective.

The revolutionary step would be dependable transfer across unfamiliar interfaces, users, and contexts within declared boundaries. An analogy to predictive engineering is useful only to that extent: a successful theory would not imply that every person's behavior is deterministic or that social context can be ignored. The supplied evidence supports the value of the research direction, but does not guarantee its eventual success or establish a historical ranking of its importance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability in the proposed innovation is an integrated model that derives useful interaction strategies from the interface, task, environment, and user's constraints while predicting both performance and its development through experience. The 2022 paper explains why manually specified strategies are restrictive: changes to a design or environment can require new rules, and different users can require different rule sets. Avoiding that dependence while retaining accurate predictions is a substantive scientific and engineering challenge.

A crucial distinction is between modeling behavior after adaptation and modeling the process of adaptation. The 2022 paper characterizes computationally rational models as accounts of adapted behavior and identifies human learning and generalization to unseen interfaces as challenges. Predicting a proficient strategy does not by itself predict a novice's exploration, mistakes, learning curve, or response to a changed interface. A broader theory must connect those trajectories to prior knowledge and experience while extending beyond local perceptual and motor tasks to context and social interaction.

Transfer also requires separating effects that persist across users and settings from effects specific to a laboratory sample or presentation method. The 2025 visual-search study identifies limitations involving its population, task, device presentation, and modeling. In particular, displaying mobile-interface screenshots on a desktop monitor does not test interaction with a mobile device. These limitations illustrate why component findings cannot simply be assembled and assumed to predict complete interactive behavior.

Proposed engineering requirements include estimating user-specific parameters without effectively relearning each interface, combining component models without losing their explanatory value, and producing calibrated uncertainty when conditions differ from those used to build the model. A convincing implementation would need explicit ways to recognize insufficient information or conditions outside its demonstrated scope. These are requirements synthesized for the proposed innovation, rather than capabilities established by the supplied papers.

current_state.text: Antti Oulasvirta, Jussi P. P. Jokinen, and Andrew Howes's CHI 2022 paper, “Computational Rationality as a Theory of Interaction” (DOI: 10.1145/3491102.3517739), develops a substantive framework for understanding interaction as adaptation under constraints. According to the supplied review of its complete main-paper text, it documents perceptual, motor, and memory components and discusses using models to evaluate hypothetical design interventions. It also identifies limitations concerning human learning, generalization, context, social interaction, and expansion from local interaction phenomena to broader HCI settings. These are dated contributions and limitations, not evidence that the full proposed capability has been achieved.

Aini Putkonen and colleagues' 2025 article, “Understanding Visual Search in Graphical User Interfaces” (DOI: 10.1016/j.ijhcs.2025.103483), reports a laboratory eye-tracking study involving 84 participants, 900 GUI screenshots, and 10,282 visual-search trials. The supplied review confirms those quantities from the main text and reports that the results prose documents effects on search time. This is evidence about visual search as one component of interaction; it does not validate predictions across complete interactive tasks, learning trajectories, device use, and social contexts.

The visual-search authors identify population, task, device-presentation, and modeling limitations and call for testing more representative populations, including greater age variation. Mobile GUIs in the study were presented on a desktop monitor. The earlier research record's PDF timeout has been superseded by the supplied review's access to the complete main-paper text, so it no longer prevents reporting the study's verified sample and trial counts. However, the review did not inspect graphical content in either article or the 2025 supplementary materials; conclusions here rely on the reviewed prose and do not assume those additional materials were examined.

Together, the supplied papers establish a theoretical foundation and a component-level empirical contribution. They do not establish a broadly predictive, independently validated theory of the scope proposed here. Conversely, the absence of a supplied freshness-search record means they cannot establish that the broader goal remained unmet throughout the field as of November 1, 2026. The present field-wide state is therefore unresolved in this record; that evidence limit does not negate the documented contributions.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: before observing users of held-out interface families, preregister quantitative predictions of learning curves, errors, task completion, and adaptation to interface changes. Specify what information the model receives about users, tasks, and designs, and distinguish predictions made from prior knowledge from those updated using new observations. Fitting historical data or reproducing proficient behavior alone would not demonstrate the proposed prospective capability.
completion_criteria.label: Preregister quantitative behavioral predictions before observing held-out interface families

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: independent teams would test those predictions across devices, task types, and diverse populations, including unfamiliar combinations of these conditions. Testing should include actual interaction as well as component tasks and should examine transfer after changes in layout, functionality, or interaction method. This breadth addresses the learning and generalization challenges discussed in the 2022 paper and the population and presentation limitations of the 2025 study. The protocol itself is a proposal, not an established standard prescribed by those sources.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams validate interaction predictions across unfamiliar conditions and changes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation requirements: define held-out interface families, specialized baseline models, performance thresholds, and uncertainty-calibration metrics before testing. Demonstrate reproducible predictive improvement over appropriate specialized models on the declared evaluation scope, while reporting failures and conditions where a specialized model performs better. Independent reproduction would require sufficient model, parameter, task, and analysis information to repeat the evaluation. No numerical threshold is established by the supplied record.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible predictive improvement over specialized models under predefined evaluation criteria

completion_criteria.text: Practical completion would mean a convincing, reproducible demonstration within explicit boundaries, with a clear account of what additional data or recalibration a new setting requires. Finite tests could establish demonstrated breadth and transfer, not literal universality across all people and interfaces. Applications such as safety-critical design assessment would require further validation tied to their own tasks and consequences.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce bounded predictions and report new-setting data or recalibration requirements

related_concepts.text: Conceptual mapping based on the supplied roster: HCI-02, “Reliable communication and computer control after profound paralysis,” and HCI-04, “An interface that makes inaccessible software operable through a user's chosen modality,” overlap through user differences, alternative input methods, and learning. A predictive science could help evaluate interaction demands and adaptation for these systems. Their defining achievements remain reliable communication or operability for intended users; predicting behavior would not itself deliver either capability.

HCI-03, “A general-purpose, high-fidelity interface for touch and physical force,” and HCI-07, “Everyday visual computing with perceptually convincing spatial displays,” overlap with the perceptual and motor foundations of HCI-01. Their devices could provide demanding settings for testing predictive models across modalities. Their core breakthroughs concern physical or perceptual interface capabilities, whereas HCI-01 concerns predicting how people use and adapt to interfaces.

HCI-05, “End-user programming that ordinary users can understand and maintain,” and HCI-06, “Delegation interfaces that keep people in meaningful control of computer work,” overlap through comprehension, learning, errors, and adaptation. HCI-01 could supply behavioral predictions for evaluating those interfaces. Understandable maintenance and meaningful control remain separate outcomes: predictive accuracy alone does not establish either one.

HCI-08, “Real-time conversational interfaces across signed and spoken languages,” and HCI-11, “Remote collaboration with usable shared social and spatial cues,” highlight language, coordination, and social context as potential tests of a broader predictive theory. Their defining goals are effective communication and collaboration. HCI-01 would seek to predict behavior in such settings, without replacing the language-processing or communication capabilities those concepts require.

HCI-09, “Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services,” and HCI-10, “Lifelong personal memory augmentation with controllable evidence,” overlap through users' understanding, prior knowledge, trust, and control. Behavioral models could help evaluate how people interpret settings or use evidence. Enforceable privacy and controllable memory evidence require separate system capabilities that cannot be inferred from successful predictions of user behavior. These roster connections are proposed conceptual relationships, not integrations demonstrated by the supplied papers.

change_log.reason: The research and review describe an integrated predictive capability whose scope extends beyond isolated component models.

change_log.change: Made the distinction between adapted behavior and the process of adaptation explicit.
change_log.reason: The review identifies this distinction as central to understanding why existing computational-rationality models do not by themselves establish predictions of learning and transfer.

change_log.reason: These limits determine how far component findings can support claims about actual interaction across devices and populations.

unresolved_issues: Whether the broader capability remained unmet as of November 1, 2026 cannot be determined from the supplied dated sources and empty freshness-search record.
The supplied review does not provide specific visual-search effect sizes or detailed result patterns; none are inferred here from its general description of search-time effects.
Graphical content in both articles and the 2025 supplementary materials were not inspected in the supplied review.
A future evaluation protocol must choose interface-family boundaries, baseline models, numerical performance thresholds, calibration metrics, and allowable user-specific adaptation.
The roster supplies titles rather than evidence about the other innovations, so their relationships to HCI-01 remain conceptual mappings rather than demonstrated integrations.

brief.title: Predicting how people use unfamiliar software
possible: Before you use a redesigned app, its designers could predict where you might struggle, which mistakes you might make and how quickly you would learn. They could also predict how changing the design would change your approach.
The same account of human behavior would work across unfamiliar kinds of software, using information about the task, the users and their setting without needing a new set of rules for each design.
why: Designers could compare proposed changes before watching people use them. Predictions would cover how people change their approach, helping designers anticipate learning difficulties and errors before release.

sources.who: Antti Oulasvirta, Jussi P. P. Jokinen and Andrew Howes
sources.showed: They brought together models that explain interaction as adaptation to limits on thought, movement and the environment. These models derive a user's strategy rather than requiring someone to write it out.
sources.cited_for: Their framework provides a basis for predicting how people respond to design changes.
sources.not_established: It does not establish dependable predictions of learning and behavior across unfamiliar interfaces and social settings.

sources.showed: They tracked people's eyes as they searched interface screenshots. Interface type, whether the target was present and how it was described affected search time more than visual complexity did.
sources.quote:
The study found 
that the type of GUI, the absence/presence of the target, and cue type affected search time more than visual 
complexity did.
sources.cited_for: The study measures how people find items on screens, one part of using software.
sources.not_established: Searching screenshots does not establish predictions for complete tasks, learning or actual mobile-device use.

shown: Oulasvirta, Jokinen and Howes developed a framework linking people's strategies to their abilities, goals and surroundings. It supports models of adapted behavior, but predicting how people reach that behavior remains a challenge.

Putkonen and colleagues measured screen-search behavior in 84 participants. Their findings describe a component of interaction; they do not demonstrate a general ability to predict how people use unfamiliar software.
missing: An integrated model must predict strategies and learning without requiring new behavioral rules for every interface.
Predictions must transfer across users, devices, tasks and social settings during actual interaction.
The model must give reliable estimates of uncertainty and recognize conditions beyond its demonstrated reach.

milestones.label: Predictions registered before unfamiliar interfaces are tested
milestones.explanation: Predictions of learning, errors, completion and adaptation would have to be registered before observing users of unfamiliar interface families. This would distinguish prediction from fitting past behavior.

milestones.label: Independent teams confirm predictions across unfamiliar conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to test actual interaction across devices, tasks, diverse users and unfamiliar combinations, including design changes. This would establish whether predictions transfer.

milestones.label: Repeatable gains over specialized models
milestones.explanation: Repeatable gains over specialized models would have to meet criteria set before testing, including uncertainty accuracy, with failures reported. Shared model and test details would allow independent repetition.

milestones.label: Repeatable predictions within clear limits
milestones.explanation: Predictions would have to be reproduced within stated boundaries, with the extra data or adjustments needed for new settings explained. This would establish usable reach without claiming universality.

uncertain: How should tests define distinct interface families and the amount of adjustment allowed for individual users?
What accuracy and uncertainty standards would make predictions useful compared with specialized models?
How well can models connect practiced behavior with a beginner's exploration, mistakes and learning?

page.title: Predictive models of human–computer interaction
page.definition: One computational model predicts task times, errors, learning and responses to design changes across unfamiliar interfaces from the design, task and user characteristics. It derives interaction strategies, meaning sequences of user actions, without new hand-written strategy rules for each interface.

goal.need: The keystroke-level model's 1980 evaluation used 28 experts and reported root-mean-square error equal to 21% of average predicted execution time under a specified action method. In 2025, measuring visual search across the interface classes below involved 84 participants and 10,282 trials. Predicting designs before user testing requires extending models beyond practiced, error-free execution to learning, mistakes and changed designs.

completion.title: Independent investigators reproduce a model's predictions across unfamiliar interface families.
completion.criterion: An independent team repeats a prospective test of the same frozen model on new users and a different interface family excluded from development. The model predicts task times, errors, learning trajectories and action choices after a design change without new strategy rules or fitting to test-interface behavior. In both studies it beats the best published task-specific comparator selected on development data for every outcome: lower mean squared error for times and learning trajectories, and lower log loss for errors and action choices.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional definition; no outside body’s acceptance test was found for this combined capability.
completion.basis: Searched NSF’s HCI solicitation, ERC Artificial User objectives, computational-rationality validation guidance, and HCI and cognitive prediction benchmarks. No shared acceptance test covering learning and transfer across unfamiliar interface families was found. This test combines the published prediction and transfer goals with independent replication. The outcome combination, comparator selection and loss functions are Atlas choices.

milestones.title: A user model improves keystroke-level prediction accuracy or relaxes the model's restrictions.
milestones.criterion: A proposed model improves on the keystroke-level model’s accuracy for comparable tasks or relaxes its restrictions: expert users, routine tasks, a method specified in detail and error-free execution. This is a comparative criterion, not a universal percentage-error threshold. The 2022 synthesis documents models that derive interaction strategies for typing, menus and task interleaving rather than requiring those strategies to be supplied.
milestones.set_by: Card, Moran and Newell, the keystroke-level model’s developers, in the conclusion of their 1980 paper.
milestones.threshold_quote: Any new proposal must do better than the Keystroke-Level Model (improve on its accuracy or lessen its restrictions) to merit serious consideration.

milestones.title: A typing simulator runs on 10 keyboard applications excluded from training.
milestones.criterion: In MobileTyping Task 3.1, train on 28 keyboard applications represented by 816 screenshots and run the simulator on 10 excluded applications represented by 212 screenshots. Assess simulated typing speed, proofreading and error correction. CRTypist reported test-set speed of 27.4 words per minute, SD 4.4. This demonstrates simulator transfer within touchscreen typing; the split itself does not establish prediction accuracy against humans on every excluded keyboard. The protocol sets no numerical acceptance tolerance.
milestones.set_by: Shi and colleagues, MobileTyping benchmark and CRTypist evaluation, Section 5.3.1, 2024; this protocol concerns touchscreen keyboards.
milestones.threshold_quote: a training set (28 keyboards, 816 screenshots) and a testing one (10 keyboards, 212 screenshots).

milestones.title: One user model predicts learning, errors and task times in an unfamiliar interface family.
milestones.criterion: One model prospectively predicts task times, error probabilities, practice trajectories and post-redesign action choices in an interface family excluded from development. No new strategy rules or fitting to that family's behavioral data are allowed. It beats the best published task-specific comparator selected on development data, using mean squared error for times and practice trajectories and log loss for errors and choices. No result meeting this combined test was located. Centaur's 2025 transfer tests concern psychological experiments, not unfamiliar interfaces; its training corpus comprised 160 experiments and 60,092 participants.
milestones.set_by: Atlas provisional definition; searches of the Artificial User objectives, HCI modeling guidance and cognitive prediction benchmarks found no equivalent cross-interface acceptance test.

not_found: No standards-body, society, agency or prize acceptance criterion was found for the combined prediction of learning and transfer across unfamiliar interface families.
No published result satisfying the combined prospective transfer and independent replication test was located.
No numerical pass/fail tolerance was found for MobileTyping’s excluded-keyboard evaluation.

results.finding: RL-KLM learned interaction strategies across 3 simulated interface cases without a prespecified action sequence.
results.detail: The model relaxes KLM’s requirement for a specified method. It also simulated recognition errors. The authors did not test its policies against empirical user data; the source identifies a conference paper but does not state its review status.
results.quote:
We report results from RL-KLM across three simple but rep-
resentative interface problems using a plain vanilla RL method
called Q-learning.

results.finding: WSTypist, evaluated with 8 agents, simulated an average uncorrected error rate of 0.05 versus 0.04 for humans.
results.detail: The model simulates typing errors and corrective actions, relaxing the keystroke-level model’s error-free execution restriction. Agents were fitted to human behavioral metrics and evaluated on 100 words each; no comparison with a keystroke-level model is reported.

results.finding: CRTypist simulated typing on 10 excluded keyboard applications: 27.4 words per minute.
results.detail: Training used 28 applications (816 screenshots); testing used 10 (212 screenshots). The study also assessed proofreading and error correction. The split alone does not establish accuracy against humans on every excluded keyboard.
